title: Piano Piano — The Sicilian Art of Patience in Paint, Soil, and Kitchen
excerpt: In Sicily, piano piano is not slowness — it is the understanding that paint, soil, and sauce all resist hurry, and reward the ones who stay.
body:
There is a phrase you hear everywhere in Sicily — at the market, in the kitchen, on the lips of every zia who ever watched you rush. Piano piano. Slowly, slowly. It is not laziness. It is the opposite. It is the knowledge that the things worth doing cannot be forced.

I think about this every time I pick up a brush. A good glaze needs the layer beneath it to dry completely. Push it, and the colors go muddy. Wait — let the pigment settle, let the surface cure — and light passes through each layer like sun through shallow water. The patience is not a delay before the result. It is the result.

The kitchen follows the same law. A proper sugo needs hours. The cipolla must go translucent before the tomato. The tomato must reduce before anything else joins. Each step has its own clock. Skip ahead and you taste the shortcut — a flatness, a sharpness that says someone was watching the time instead of the pot.

And in the garden, patience is not optional. It is the entire contract you sign with the earth. You plant rosemary in spring and wait. You water basil every morning and watch. A seed does not negotiate. It will come when it comes, and all you can do is show up.

What I find beautiful is that all three — painting, cooking, growing — teach the same lesson through different materials. Oil paint, tomato sauce, and soil all resist hurry. They reward attention. They punish distraction. And each one produces something that nourishes.

## The science of slowing down

This is not only poetry. A 2016 study from the University of Otago, published in the *Journal of Positive Psychology*, followed 658 young adults over 13 days and found that people who spent time on creative activities — including cooking and gardening — reported significantly higher positive affect and a sense of "flourishing" the following day. The benefit came not from what was produced, but from the process: sustained, focused attention that psychologists call flow.

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, the psychologist who originated the concept of flow, described it as a state where challenge and skill meet in perfect balance. Time slows. Self-consciousness drops. The work becomes its own reward. Anyone who has lost an afternoon at the easel or spent a morning pruning without checking the clock knows this feeling. It is piano piano made visible.

The PREDIMED trial — one of the largest randomized nutrition studies conducted, published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* — showed that a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil reduced major cardiovascular events by approximately 30 percent. But what the headlines often miss is that the diet cannot be separated from the way of eating: slowly, seasonally, socially. The food is the vehicle. The pace is part of the medicine.

## Where the three meet

In Palermo, you see this convergence in the old markets — Ballarò, il Capo, la Vucciria. A fishmonger arranges his catch like a still life. A vendor stacks blood oranges in a pyramid that could hold its own in any gallery. The colors are deliberate. The composition matters. Nobody is rushing, and the care shows in everything.

This is what I try to carry into my own days. I grow the basil. I cook the pesto. I paint the bowl it sits in. Each step slow, each step complete on its own, each step feeding the next. The [garden](/giardino) becomes the [kitchen](/cucina) becomes the studio, and all of it — piano piano — becomes a way of living that holds together.

Sicily teaches this. The light teaches patience because it changes every hour. The soil teaches patience because it gives on its own calendar. The kitchen teaches patience because a good sugo will not be rushed. And the canvas teaches patience because it remembers every hurried mark.

Piano piano. The slow way is the only way that lasts.
author: Milly Farfalla
